usefulness.example: A 300-student lab submits add.c / sum_array.c. The instructor drops the rules file and test folder next to the submissions and batch-grades them with `python manage.py grade submissions/*.c --rules rules/add_two_integers.json` in a few minutes.
usefulness.benefit: Every student gets the same rubric and a per-metric breakdown with the exact failing input (e.g. 2147483647 1 -> expected 2147483648) instead of a bare mark.

usefulness.example: A company screens 500 candidates on 'sum an array safely in O(n)'. Candidates with an O(n^2) nested loop are separated by the timing curve, and those with int accumulators by the int_overflow corner cases.
usefulness.benefit: Fast first-round filtering where every rejection can be justified metric by metric with stored evidence.

usefulness.example: Two submissions reach 0.93 abstract-structure similarity (> 0.85 threshold) although every variable was renamed and a for-loop rewritten as a while-loop; a third matches a qwen3-generated solution. Only these are flagged.
usefulness.benefit: Instructors review a handful of flagged pairs instead of reading all submissions.

usefulness.example: A student uploads sum_leak.c at midnight; the report shows 'memory-leak at line 14: 400 bytes leaked (macOS leaks)' and a WHY/AI-tutor explanation of the failing case, so they fix it before the deadline.
usefulness.benefit: Teaching-assistant style feedback (ASan/UBSan, leaks, counterexamples) available 24/7 without staff time.

limitations.example: A submission that special-cases the inputs it has seen (e.g. `if (a == 7 && b == 5) puts("12");` for every hidden test) or that only fails for n = 99991 passes all hidden tests and all generated corner cases and gets a full correctness score.
limitations.mitigation: Seeded random + LLM-proposed counter-tests are judged against the reference solution, but coverage is still finite; keep hidden tests secret and rotate them.

limitations.limitation: Timing-based complexity is unreliable for small inputs
limitations.example: An O(n^2) solution on sizes [1, 10, 100] runs in < 1 ms at every size; the curve is flat, so the agent falls back to static loop nesting. A loop like `for (i = 0; i < 3; i++)` is counted as O(n) nesting and a recursive merge sort is treated as possibly exponential, giving a wrong complexity verdict.
limitations.mitigation: Use large sizes (e.g. 10^3..10^6) in the rules, and min-of-N CPU time; treat the complexity score as advisory near class boundaries.

limitations.limitation: Similarity cannot judge tiny programs and can miss semantic rewrites
limitations.example: For add_two_integers almost every token k-gram is shared with the reference solution, so a copied 6-line program is reported as 'too little unique code to judge' and gets 10/10 originality. Conversely, a copy translated into a different algorithm (recursion instead of a loop) scores low similarity and is not flagged.
limitations.mitigation: Base-code exclusion avoids false positives, but originality is only meaningful for programs with real logic; flags require human review, never automatic penalties.

limitations.limitation: Verdicts depend on the compiler and platform
limitations.example: `while (b != 0) { s += 1; }` never terminates when b != 0, but clang -O2 is allowed (C11 6.8.5p6) to delete the side-effect-free loop, so the smoke run finishes in 6 ms and the agent reports a wrong answer instead of an infinite loop. On macOS RLIMIT_AS is ignored, so the memory cap is enforced by polling: a program that allocates 200 MB and exits within ~5 ms can pass a 64 MB limit, and leaks are only checked (with `leaks`) on the first two inputs.
limitations.mitigation: Grade on Linux in a container (RLIMIT_AS, LeakSanitizer/valgrind), pin compiler + flags in the rules; tool_versions are recorded in every report.
